title: Classification of Administrative Functions — Legislative, Executive, Judicial and Quasi-Judicial

content.overview: Administrative action is classified as legislative, executive, judicial or quasi-judicial. The classification is functional, not formal. It determines the applicable procedural safeguards (especially natural justice) and the intensity of judicial review.
content.glance: Identify the nature of the power; apply the functional tests (policy vs individualised determination; rights vs privileges; lis); state the consequence for natural justice and review standards.
content.study: Modern administration combines rule-making, pure executive action and adjudicatory functions. Courts classify the function by looking at its nature and effect rather than the label used by the statute. Legislative functions produce general rules of conduct; pure executive functions involve policy or managerial discretion without a lis; quasi-judicial functions decide disputed questions affecting individual rights and attract natural-justice requirements. The distinction is critical for audi alteram partem, reasoned orders and the scope of judicial review. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the parent statute and constitutional standards. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Why Classification Matters
sections.body: Classification controls the applicability of natural justice, the duty to give reasons, and the intensity of judicial review.

sections.heading: Legislative Functions
sections.body: Rule-making that produces general norms of conduct. Publication and ultra-vires review are principal controls; full natural justice is ordinarily not required.

sections.heading: Pure Executive Functions
sections.body: Policy, managerial or discretionary action without a lis between parties. Fairness may still constrain the action under Article 14, but classical natural-justice templates are often inapplicable.

sections.heading: Judicial and Quasi-Judicial Functions
sections.body: Determination of disputed questions affecting individual rights. A lis, duty to act judicially, and consequences for the person supply the indicators. Natural justice applies.

sections.heading: Functional Tests
sections.body: Courts examine the nature of the power, the presence of a dispute, the effect on rights, and statutory indicators rather than formal labels.

sections.heading: Consequences for Review
sections.body: Quasi-judicial decisions attract stricter procedural review; legislative instruments are tested mainly for ultra vires and constitutional validity; pure executive action is reviewed for arbitrariness and relevant considerations.

examples.title: Rule-making vs adjudication
examples.body: An authority frames a general fee schedule applicable to all licensees (legislative). Separately it cancels one licensee’s permit after a contested inquiry (quasi-judicial). Natural justice applies to the cancellation, not to the fee schedule.

examples.title: Policy decision without lis
examples.body: Government decides to close a public sector unit for economic reasons. No individualised dispute is decided. The action is executive; challenge proceeds on arbitrariness or relevant-considerations grounds rather than classical natural-justice failure.

examples.title: Selection with bias indicators
examples.body: A selection committee includes a person who is himself a candidate. The function is quasi-judicial; the presence of bias attracts the nemo judex principle.

hypotheticals.question: Does the label ‘administrative’ exclude natural justice?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Classification is functional. If the action decides a contested claim affecting rights, natural justice applies regardless of the statutory label.

hypotheticals.question: Are all policy decisions immune from fairness review?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Article 14 non-arbitrariness and legitimate-expectation doctrines may still constrain pure executive policy decisions.

hypotheticals.question: Is rule-making always free of hearing requirements?
hypotheticals.analysis: Generally yes for pure legislative functions, but statute or fairness may require consultation in particular contexts.

distinctions.title: Legislative vs quasi-judicial function
distinctions.right: Individualised determination of existing rights or liabilities

distinctions.title: Pure executive vs quasi-judicial
distinctions.left: Policy or managerial discretion without a lis
distinctions.right: Decision of a disputed question affecting rights

rows.right: Lis and duty to act judicially

misconceptions.trap: The statutory label ‘administrative’ decides the classification.
misconceptions.correction: Classification is functional; courts look at the nature and effect of the power.

misconceptions.trap: Natural justice never applies to administrative action.
misconceptions.correction: Quasi-judicial administrative action attracts natural justice; pure executive action is still constrained by Article 14 fairness.

misconceptions.trap: All rule-making requires a prior hearing of every affected person.
misconceptions.correction: Pure legislative functions ordinarily do not; individualised determinations do.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a classification-of-functions problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the power and its effect. II. Apply functional tests (policy vs individualised determination; lis; rights). III. Classify the function. IV. State the procedural and review consequences. V. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions on functional classification contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Nature of the power; presence or absence of a lis; effect on rights; applicable natural-justice or Article 14 standard; precise relief.

enhancement.definition: Administrative functions are classified as legislative, pure executive, judicial or quasi-judicial according to their nature and effect, not their statutory label.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Classification is functional; quasi-judicial action attracts natural justice; pure executive action remains subject to Article 14 fairness; legislative action is controlled mainly by ultra vires and constitutional limits.
essentialIngredients: Presence or absence of a lis
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Courts look at the substance of the power. Individualised determinations affecting rights are quasi-judicial; general rule-making is legislative; policy without a lis is pure executive.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the power; apply functional tests; classify; state natural-justice and review consequences.
keyTakeaways: Pure executive action is still constrained by Article 14.
Legislative functions are reviewed mainly for ultra vires.
